rules.rule: Do not stop at saying something was interesting; explain what was new and why it matters.
rules.reason: The professor pushed students past vague impressions toward explicit comparison between prior assumptions and new understanding.

rules.rule: Distinguish close terms precisely and include the English label when relevant.
rules.reason: The class explicitly separated gerontology from geriatrics rather than treating them as loose synonyms.

rules.rule: When giving historical or institutional background, name the concrete actor and context instead of using broad labels.
rules.reason: Answers like "the West" or "the pension system" were pushed toward Bismarck, Germany, and the historical pension context.

rules.rule: Explain age categories as socially constructed criteria, not as self-evident natural facts.
rules.reason: The 65-year threshold was framed as a historical policy construction rather than a scientific cut point.

rules.rule: If the reading uses a catchy label, explain the direction behind it instead of relying on the label itself.
rules.reason: The professor said that the framing behind "new gerontology" matters more than repeating the term as if it were a standard classroom keyword.

rules.rule: Keep both sides of aging in view; avoid answers that romanticize old age or reduce it to decline only.
rules.reason: The professor repeatedly stressed that strong answers balance limits, decline, possibility, and variation instead of choosing one extreme frame.

rules.rule: Use the exact age concept being discussed and define it clearly.
rules.reason: The class moved from vague calendar-age wording toward exact labels such as chronological age and different age dimensions.

rules.rule: Separate answers about individual aging processes from answers about older-adult groups or social categories.
rules.reason: The professor explicitly distinguished focus on personal aging processes from focus on age-defined groups and linked that split to disciplinary perspective.
